summary: Full of the Spirit, Jesus is tested in the wilderness over sonship, bread, rule, worship, and spectacular protection. Luke orders the final temptation at Jerusalem, the city toward which the Gospel will travel. In Nazareth Jesus reads a composite Isaiah passage announcing Spirit, good news to the poor, release, sight, and favor, then says it is fulfilled ‘today.’ Hometown approval turns to rage when Elijah and Elisha expose grace beyond familiar claims. Jesus passes through them, teaches with authority in Capernaum, frees a man from an unclean spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others, withdraws, and insists he ‘must’ proclaim God's kingdom to other cities.
whyItMatters: Luke's program is public and concrete: Spirit-anointed good news brings release and restoration while refusing hometown ownership. Jesus rejects power gained through appetite, idolatry, or spectacle and defines necessity as carrying God's kingdom beyond the place that thinks it possesses him.

keyVerses.text: “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed,
keyVerses.why: Luke gives Jesus's Spirit-anointed mission its vocabulary of good news and release.

keyVerses.text: He began to tell them, “Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
keyVerses.why: Promise becomes a present event addressed to hearers who must decide how to receive it.

keyVerses.text: But he said to them, “I must preach the good news of God’s Kingdom to the other cities also. For this reason I have been sent.”
keyVerses.why: Divine necessity refuses local possession and pushes the mission outward.

questions.question: Why does Luke place the Jerusalem temptation last?
questions.answer: Matthew ends on a mountain; Luke ends at the temple in Jerusalem, the destination governing both volumes. The devil's scriptural test anticipates later pressure to prove sonship spectacularly. Luke changes sequence for narrative theology without claiming the other order never circulated.

questions.question: Does ‘if you are the Son of God’ mean the devil doubts Jesus's identity?
questions.answer: The Greek condition can carry ‘since’ as well as skeptical ‘if.’ After the baptismal voice, the tests target how sonship will be exercised: self-provision, rule by worshiping evil, and forcing divine rescue. Jesus answers from Deuteronomy as a faithful Israelite Son in the wilderness.

questions.question: Is Jesus reading one continuous Isaiah passage?
questions.answer: The wording draws chiefly from Isaiah 61:1–2 with a line resembling Isaiah 58:6 and omits the vengeance line after ‘the acceptable year.’ Luke presents a scriptural composition, not a modern quotation with ellipses. Release, sight, good news, and favor interpret one another.

questions.question: What does aphesis, translated ‘release,’ contribute?
questions.answer: Aphesis can name liberation, cancellation, remission, or forgiveness. Luke uses it for captives here and for forgiveness of sins elsewhere. The shared word prevents readers from isolating spiritual forgiveness from freedom imagery, while context keeps every use from meaning exactly the same thing.

questions.question: Why does the hometown crowd turn from admiration to violence?
questions.answer: Jesus refuses to turn familiarity into entitlement. Elijah aided a Sidonian widow and Elisha healed a Syrian while need remained in Israel; the examples expose grace that crosses borders and judgment on resistant insiders. The scene is not ‘Jews reject Gentiles’: Jesus, prophets, synagogue, and examples all belong to Israel's own argument.

questions.question: Did Jesus literally escape by becoming invisible?
questions.answer: Luke says he passed through the middle of the crowd and went away, without describing a miracle mechanism. Divine protection, commanding presence, crowd hesitation, or narrative compression are possible readings. Claims about invisibility go beyond the words.

questions.question: Why do demons recognize Jesus when people do not?
questions.answer: The unclean spirit names ‘the Holy One of God,’ and later demons call him Christ, but Jesus silences them. Accurate labels are not faithful witness, and hostile testimony does not control his identity. Luke lets deeds, teaching, cross, resurrection, and commissioned witnesses disclose who he is.

questions.question: What does Simon's mother-in-law do after healing, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: She immediately rises and serves the household. That is not evidence that women exist to wait on men; it is Luke's compact sign of complete restoration and responsive hospitality. Later Jesus describes his own leadership with the same service logic.

glossary.def: Peirazō can mean entice toward evil or test; the scene exposes what kind of Son Jesus will be.
